lessons.title: The employment relationship and contract
lessons.html:
Who is an employer and who is an employee?

The employer is the person or business that gives work and pays wages, for example the stud farm owner or the training yard. The employee is the person who does the work and gets paid. The two have an agreement. Each side has duties and rights.

The contract of employment

A contract is an agreement. It can be spoken or written, but a written contract is better because both sides can check it. The employer must give the employee written details of employment. These details include:

  • Names of the employer and employee
  • Job title and description of the work
  • Place of work
  • Starting date
  • Working hours and days
  • Wage and how often it is paid
  • Leave
  • Notice period to end the job

Read the contract before you sign. Ask questions about anything you do not understand. Keep your copy safe.

Laws that protect workers

  • Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 - working hours, overtime, leave, payslips, notice
  • Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 - fair dismissal, unions, disputes, the CCMA
  • Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 - safety at work
  • Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998 - no unfair discrimination

Farm workers are also covered by the national minimum wage and special rules for the farm sector. Your supervisor or the Department of Employment and Labour can tell you the current amounts.

The payslip

Every payday you should get a payslip. It shows your pay, the hours worked, overtime, and deductions such as UIF. Check it every time. If something is wrong, ask politely.

lessons.title: Rights, duties and solving problems
lessons.html:
Duties of the employee

  • Come to work on time and do the work agreed
  • Follow reasonable instructions
  • Look after the employer's property, horses and equipment
  • Work safely and follow the rules
  • Be honest
  • Tell your supervisor if you are sick and cannot come to work

Duties of the employer

  • Pay the agreed wage on time
  • Give a safe workplace and protective clothing
  • Give leave as the law says
  • Treat workers fairly and with respect
  • Register workers for UIF and pay contributions

Your rights

  • Fair treatment without discrimination
  • To join a trade union if you want to
  • Annual leave, sick leave and family responsibility leave
  • A fair process before you are disciplined or dismissed

Discipline

Most workplaces have a disciplinary code. It lists offences such as coming late, being drunk at work, stealing, or hurting an animal. Small problems usually get a verbal or written warning first. Serious offences can lead to a hearing. You have the right to hear what you are accused of, to tell your side and to have a co-worker or union representative help you.

Grievances

A grievance is a complaint by a worker. If you feel you are treated unfairly:

  1. Speak to your supervisor calmly first.
  2. If it is not solved, follow the grievance procedure: often a written complaint to the manager.
  3. If still not solved, you can get help from a union or refer the dispute to the CCMA (Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration). The CCMA does not charge workers.

A good working relationship

Respect works both ways. Talk early about small problems before they grow. Keep promises. Example: Lindiwe's pay was short by two overtime hours. She showed the yard manager her time sheet. He checked, agreed and fixed it next payday. Calm talk solved it.

Key points

  • The employer gives work and pay; the employee does the agreed work.
  • Get written details of employment and read before you sign.
  • The BCEA and LRA protect workers' basic conditions and fair treatment.
  • Check your payslip every payday.
  • Raise grievances calmly, follow the procedure, and use the CCMA if needed.
